PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Plants are living things, just like people and animals. In this sub-strand you will find out how we know that plants are alive, name the external parts of a plant and learn what each part does. You will also learn why we must take care of plants and how you can do it at school and at home.

## Strand 1.0: Living Things and their Environment
Sub-strand 1.1: Plants
Suggested lessons: 12

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify characteristics of plants as living things
b) describe functions of external parts of plants
c) appreciate the need to care for plants

## What this sub-strand covers
• Characteristics of plants as living things
• Functions of external parts of plants

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why are plants grouped as living things?

## Core competencies
• Communication and Collaboration: The learner develops speaking and listening skills as they discuss the functions of external parts of plants.
• Digital literacy: The learner develops manipulative skills as they interact with digital media to draw, paint and label external parts of a plant.

## Values
• Unity: The learner cooperates in taking turns while they observe young plants/seedlings, draw and label their parts and share with peers.
• Respect: The learner listens to and appreciates others’ opinions during discussions on the characteristics of plants.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Safety and Security: The learner observes safety while handling different types of plants as they take a walk in the school compound and adjacent environment to observe, discuss and record characteristics of plants as living things.

## Links to other learning areas
• Agriculture and Nutrition: The learner uses information on characteristics of plants as living things in the study of different types of crops.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Science and Technology Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 1.0 Living Things and their Environment, Sub-strand 1.1 Plants

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Plants are living things

LESSON 1: PLANTS ARE LIVING THINGS
==================================

## What you will learn
• State the characteristics that show plants are living things.
• Tell the difference between a living plant and a non-living object.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify characteristics of plants as living things

## Introduction
Put a stone and a bean seed in wet soil and wait two weeks. The stone stays the same, but the bean seed sprouts and grows leaves. What makes the bean seed different from the stone?

## Notes
Everything around us is either living or non-living. A stone, a chair and a plastic bottle are non-living. A dog, a person and a mango tree are living. Plants are grouped as living things because they show the characteristics of life.

### Characteristics of plants as living things
- **Plants grow.** A small maize seedling becomes a tall maize plant. A young tree gets taller and its stem becomes thicker every year.
- **Plants reproduce.** Reproduce means to make new plants of the same kind. Beans produce seeds that grow into new bean plants. Sugarcane and cassava can grow from pieces of stem planted in the soil. Sweet potatoes can grow from vines.
- **Plants remove waste.** Plants give out extra water as water vapour through their leaves. They also give out oxygen, which is left over when they make food. Some plants shed old leaves.
- **Plants respond to changes in their environment.** A plant kept near a window bends its stem towards the light. Roots grow towards water in the soil. The leaves of the touch-me-not plant (mimosa) fold up quickly when you touch them.
- **Plants die.** When a plant gets old, or lacks water for a long time, it dries up and dies. Maize plants dry up after the maize is harvested.

Plants also need food, water and air to stay alive. Unlike animals, green plants make their own food in their leaves using sunlight, water and air.

### How is a plant different from a non-living thing?
A non-living thing such as a stone does not grow, does not reproduce, does not remove waste, does not respond to changes and does not die. A plant does all of these things.

Plants do not move from place to place like animals, but their parts move slowly: leaves turn towards light and roots grow deeper into the soil.

## Key words
• living thing — something that grows, reproduces, removes waste, responds to changes and dies
• reproduce — to make new young ones of the same kind
• respond — to react to a change around it, such as light or touch
• seedling — a young plant that has just grown from a seed

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A potted plant placed near a window bends towards the window after a few days. Which characteristic of living things does this show?

Working:
1. The plant is reacting to light coming through the window.
2. Reacting to a change around you is called responding.

Answer: Plants respond to changes in their environment.

### Example 2
A farmer plants maize seeds. Some months later there are new maize cobs with many seeds. Which characteristic does this show?

Working:
1. New seeds that can grow into new maize plants have been made.
2. Making new plants of the same kind is reproduction.

Answer: Plants reproduce.

## Activity: Nature walk: evidence that plants are alive
You will need: Notebook and pencil, A hand lens if available
1. Walk in a group around the school compound with your teacher.
2. Look for evidence that plants grow (seedlings, new leaves), reproduce (flowers, fruits, seeds), remove waste (fallen leaves), respond (plants bending towards light) and die (dry plants).
3. Record what you see in a table with two columns: Characteristic and Evidence.
4. Do not pull up or damage plants. Do not touch thorny, stinging or unknown plants, and wash your hands after the walk.
5. Share your table with another group.

## Practice
1. List five characteristics that show plants are living things.
2. The leaves of a touch-me-not plant fold when touched. What does this show?
3. Give one way in which plants remove waste.
4. Why is a stone not a living thing?

## Summary
• Plants are living things.
• Plants grow, reproduce, remove waste, respond to changes in their environment and die.
• Green plants make their own food using sunlight, water and air.

### Answers to practice
1. Plants grow, reproduce, remove waste, respond to changes in their environment and die.
2. Plants respond to changes in their environment.
3. They give out extra water as water vapour through their leaves (or give out oxygen, or shed old leaves).
4. It does not grow, reproduce, remove waste, respond to changes or die.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: External parts of a plant

LESSON 2: EXTERNAL PARTS OF A PLANT
===================================

## What you will learn
• Name the external parts of a plant.
• Draw and label a young plant.

Curriculum outcomes: b) describe functions of external parts of plants

## Introduction
Pull a bean seedling gently out of wet soil and wash off the soil. You can see a part that was under the ground and parts that were above it. Each of these parts has a name.

## Notes
The parts of a plant that we can see from outside are called external parts. The main external parts of a plant are:

- **Roots** – the part that grows under the soil. Roots are usually white or brown and have many thin branches called root hairs near their tips.
- **Stem** – the part that grows above the soil and holds up the leaves, flowers and fruits. The stem of a bean seedling is thin and green. The stem of a tree is hard and woody and is called a trunk.
- **Leaves** – the flat, usually green parts that grow from the stem. Most leaves have a stalk that joins them to the stem and lines called veins.
- **Flowers** – the often brightly coloured parts that grow on many plants when they are old enough.
- **Fruits and seeds** – fruits grow from flowers and carry seeds inside them. Mangoes, oranges, bean pods and tomatoes are fruits.

### Looking at a young plant
A seedling is a young plant. When you look at a bean or maize seedling you will clearly see the roots, the stem and the leaves. Seedlings do not yet have flowers or fruits. These come later as the plant grows.

### Drawing and labelling
When you draw a plant:
- Use a sharp pencil and draw clear, single lines.
- Draw the soil line so it is clear which part is under the ground.
- Write the labels on the side and join each label to the part with a straight line.
- Give your drawing a title, for example A bean seedling.

Not all plants look the same. A maize plant has many thin roots of about the same size, while a bean plant has one main root with smaller roots growing from it. The leaves of maize are long and narrow, while bean leaves are wide.

## Key words
• external parts — the parts of a plant we can see from outside
• roots — the part of a plant that grows under the soil
• stem — the part of a plant that holds up leaves, flowers and fruits
• label — a name written next to a part in a drawing

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner digs up a maize seedling and sees many thin white threads under the ground. Which part is this?

Working:
1. The part is under the soil.
2. The part of a plant under the soil is the root.

Answer: Roots

## Activity: Draw and label a seedling
You will need: Bean or maize seedlings grown in a tin or dug up carefully, Water to wash off soil, Pencil, paper or exercise book, A computer or tablet with a drawing application, if available
1. In pairs, take turns to hold the seedling and observe its roots, stem and leaves.
2. Draw the seedling and label the roots, stem and leaves.
3. If your school has a computer or tablet, use a drawing application to draw, paint and label the parts of a plant.
4. Share your drawing with your peers and check each other's labels.
5. Replant the seedling or put it in the school compost when done.

## Practice
1. Name three external parts that you can see on a bean seedling.
2. Which part of a plant grows from a flower and carries seeds?
3. What do we call the hard, woody stem of a tree?

## Summary
• The external parts of a plant are the roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds.
• A seedling has roots, a stem and leaves.
• Label drawings with straight lines and clear names.

### Answers to practice
1. Roots, stem and leaves.
2. The fruit.
3. A trunk.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Functions of the external parts of a plant

LESSON 3: FUNCTIONS OF THE EXTERNAL PARTS OF A PLANT
====================================================

## What you will learn
• Describe the work of roots, stems, leaves, flowers and fruits.
• Give examples of plant parts that store food.

Curriculum outcomes: b) describe functions of external parts of plants

## Introduction
When you eat cassava, you are eating a root. When you chew sugarcane, you are chewing a stem. When you eat sukuma wiki, you are eating leaves. Every part of a plant has work to do for the plant.

## Notes
Each external part of a plant has a function. A function is the work that a part does.

### Roots
- Hold the plant firmly in the soil so that wind and rain do not knock it over.
- Take in (absorb) water and mineral salts from the soil.
- Some roots store food for the plant. Carrots, cassava and sweet potatoes are roots that store food, which is why we eat them.

### Stem
- Holds up the leaves so that they get sunlight, and holds up flowers and fruits.
- Carries water and mineral salts from the roots up to the leaves, and carries food made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.
- Some stems store food. Sugarcane stores sugar in its stem. An Irish potato is a swollen underground stem that stores food.

### Leaves
- Make food for the plant using sunlight, water and air. This is why most leaves are green, flat and wide: they catch plenty of sunlight.
- Allow air to move in and out of the plant through tiny openings.
- Give out extra water as water vapour.
- Some leaves are eaten as vegetables, such as sukuma wiki (kales), cabbage, spinach and cowpea leaves.

### Flowers
- Flowers are the parts used for reproduction. After a flower is pollinated, part of it grows into a fruit with seeds. Bright colours and sweet smells attract insects such as bees, which help in pollination.

### Fruits and seeds
- Fruits protect the seeds inside them.
- Seeds grow into new plants. Many fruits are eaten by animals and people, which helps to spread the seeds to new places.

All the parts work together. If the roots are cut, the leaves cannot get water and the plant wilts. If all the leaves are removed, the plant cannot make food.

## Key words
• function — the work that a part does
• absorb — to take in, as roots take in water from the soil
• mineral salts — substances in the soil that plants need to grow well
• wilt — to droop and go soft because of lack of water

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner puts a white flower with its stalk into a cup of water mixed with ink. After a day the petals have coloured lines. What does this show about the stem?

Working:
1. The coloured water moved up from the cup into the petals.
2. It travelled through the stem.

Answer: The stem carries water from the bottom of the plant to other parts.

### Example 2
Which part of each of these plants do we eat: cassava, sugarcane, sukuma wiki?

Working:
1. Cassava grows under the soil and stores food: root.
2. Sugarcane stores sugar in its tall stem: stem.
3. Sukuma wiki is eaten for its leaves: leaves.

Answer: Cassava – root, sugarcane – stem, sukuma wiki – leaves.

## Activity: Parts and their work
You will need: A whole weed or seedling with roots, A white flower or celery stalk, a cup of water and ink or food colour, Chart paper
1. In groups, observe the plant and point to each external part.
2. Put the flower or celery stalk in coloured water and leave it until the next lesson. Observe what happens.
3. Discuss the function of each part and write it on a chart: roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruits.
4. Present your chart to the class and listen to other groups' ideas.

## Practice
1. Give two functions of roots.
2. Which part of a plant makes food?
3. Why do many flowers have bright colours and sweet smells?
4. Name one stem that stores food.

## Summary
• Roots hold the plant and absorb water and mineral salts.
• The stem holds up the plant and carries water and food.
• Leaves make food; flowers help the plant reproduce; fruits protect seeds.

### Answers to practice
1. They hold the plant firmly in the soil and absorb water and mineral salts. Some also store food.
2. The leaves.
3. To attract insects such as bees that help in pollination.
4. Sugarcane (or Irish potato).

PAGE 5: Lesson 4: Caring for plants

LESSON 4: CARING FOR PLANTS
===========================

## What you will learn
• Explain why plants are important to people and animals.
• Describe ways of caring for plants at school and at home.

Curriculum outcomes: c) appreciate the need to care for plants

## Introduction
Think about your breakfast, your desk and the shade where you rest at break time. Plants gave you most of these things. If we want plants to keep helping us, we must take care of them.

## Notes
### Why we need plants
- **Food.** We eat roots (cassava, carrots), stems (sugarcane), leaves (sukuma wiki, spinach), fruits (mangoes, bananas) and seeds (maize, beans). Animals such as cows and goats feed on grass and leaves.
- **Air.** Green plants give out oxygen, which people and animals need to breathe.
- **Shade and shelter.** Trees give shade and act as windbreaks. Birds and many small animals live in trees.
- **Materials.** Timber for desks and houses, firewood, and fibres such as sisal and cotton come from plants.
- **Medicine.** Some medicines are made from plants.
- **Soil and water.** Roots hold soil together so that rain does not wash it away. Trees help protect the sources of rivers and streams.
- **Beauty.** Flowers and hedges make our compounds beautiful.

### How to care for plants
- Water young plants, especially in the dry season. Water in the morning or evening when it is cooler.
- Put mulch (dry grass or leaves) around plants to keep the soil moist.
- Add manure or compost so that plants get what they need to grow.
- Remove weeds that compete with plants for water and space.
- Put a fence or thorny branches around young trees to protect them from animals.
- Walk on paths and do not step on flower beds or seedlings.
- Do not pluck flowers, peel bark or break branches for fun.
- Plant new trees, especially to replace ones that have been cut down.

### Staying safe around plants
Some plants have thorns, sting (like the stinging nettle) or are poisonous. Do not touch or taste a plant you do not know, and wash your hands after working with plants.

## Key words
• mulch — dry grass or leaves spread on the soil around plants to keep it moist
• weed — a plant growing where it is not wanted
• windbreak — a line of trees or hedge that slows down strong wind

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The school has planted young trees near the playground, but goats keep eating them. Suggest a way to care for the trees.

Working:
1. The problem is animals eating the young trees.
2. The trees need protection until they are big.

Answer: Put a fence or thorny branches around each young tree.

## Activity: Adopt a plant
You will need: A young tree or potted plant in the school compound, Watering can or a used bottle, Dry grass for mulch
1. In your group, choose one young plant in the school compound to care for.
2. Remove the weeds around it, water it and spread mulch around it.
3. Make a simple chart to record each time you water it and how tall it grows.
4. Take turns so that every group member cares for the plant.
5. Tell the class how your plant changes over a few weeks.

## Practice
1. Give three reasons why plants are important.
2. Why should we put mulch around plants?
3. Name two things you should not do to plants in the school compound.

## Summary
• Plants give us food, oxygen, shade, materials and medicine.
• Care for plants by watering, mulching, weeding, adding manure and protecting them.
• Do not touch or taste plants you do not know.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: they give food, oxygen, shade, timber and firewood, medicine, they hold soil together, they make places beautiful.
2. Mulch keeps the soil moist so the plant does not dry up.
3. Any two: step on seedlings or flower beds, pluck flowers, peel bark, break branches.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 1.1 PLANTS
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which of these is a living thing?
   A. A stone
   B. A plastic bottle
   C. A bean plant
   D. A desk

2. A plant near a window bends towards the light. This shows that plants:
   A. reproduce
   B. respond to changes
   C. die
   D. remove waste

3. Name the characteristic of living things shown when a maize plant dries up after harvest.

4. Which part of a plant holds it firmly in the soil?
   A. Leaf
   B. Flower
   C. Root
   D. Fruit

5. Which part of a plant makes food?
   A. Leaves
   B. Roots
   C. Seeds
   D. Flowers

6. Water moves from the roots to the leaves through the:
   A. flower
   B. stem
   C. fruit
   D. seed

7. Cassava and carrots are examples of plant parts that store food. Which part are they?
   A. Stems
   B. Leaves
   C. Roots
   D. Flowers

8. What is the main function of a flower?

9. Which of these is a good way of caring for plants?
   A. Plucking flowers
   B. Stepping on seedlings
   C. Mulching and watering
   D. Peeling bark

10. Give two reasons why we should care for plants.
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 1.1 PLANTS
========================================

1. C. A bean plant
   A bean plant grows, reproduces, removes waste, responds to changes and dies.

2. B. respond to changes
   Bending towards light is a response to a change in the environment.

3. Plants die.
   All living things die at the end of their lives.

4. C. Root
   Roots grow into the soil and anchor the plant.

5. A. Leaves
   Green leaves make food using sunlight, water and air.

6. B. stem
   The stem carries water and mineral salts up from the roots.

7. C. Roots
   Cassava and carrots are roots that store food.

8. Reproduction – it develops into a fruit with seeds.
   After pollination, part of the flower grows into a fruit that carries seeds.

9. C. Mulching and watering
   Mulching keeps soil moist and watering gives the plant the water it needs.

10. Any two: plants give us food, oxygen, shade, timber, firewood, medicine, and they hold soil together.
   People and animals depend on plants in many ways.

===================================

• Name the external parts of a plant.

- Give your drawing a title, for example A bean seedling.

## Key words
• external parts — the parts of a plant we can see from outside
• roots — the part of a plant that grows under the soil
• stem — the part of a plant that holds up leaves, flowers and fruits
• label — a name written next to a part in a drawing

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner digs up a maize seedling and sees many thin white threads under the ground. Which part is this?

Working:
1. The part is under the soil.
2. The part of a plant under the soil is the root.

Answer: Roots

## Activity: Draw and label a seedling
You will need: Bean or maize seedlings grown in a tin or dug up carefully, Water to wash off soil, Pencil, paper or exercise book, A computer or tablet with a drawing application, if available
1. In pairs, take turns to hold the seedling and observe its roots, stem and leaves.
2. Draw the seedling and label the roots, stem and leaves.
3. If your school has a computer or tablet, use a drawing application to draw, paint and label the parts of a plant.
4. Share your drawing with your peers and check each other's labels.
5. Replant the seedling or put it in the school compost when done.

## Practice
1. Name three external parts that you can see on a bean seedling.
2. Which part of a plant grows from a flower and carries seeds?
3. What do we call the hard, woody stem of a tree?

## Summary
• The external parts of a plant are the roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds.
• A seedling has roots, a stem and leaves.
• Label drawings with straight lines and clear names.

### Answers to practice
1. Roots, stem and leaves.
2. The fruit.
3. A trunk.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Functions of the external parts of a plant
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: FUNCTIONS OF THE EXTERNAL PARTS OF A PLANT
====================================================

## What you will learn
• Describe the work of roots, stems, leaves, flowers and fruits.
• Give examples of plant parts that store food.

Curriculum outcomes: b) describe functions of external parts of plants

## Introduction
When you eat cassava, you are eating a root. When you chew sugarcane, you are chewing a stem. When you eat sukuma wiki, you are eating leaves. Every part of a plant has work to do for the plant.

## Notes
Each external part of a plant has a function. A function is the work that a part does.

### Roots
- Hold the plant firmly in the soil so that wind and rain do not knock it over.
- Take in (absorb) water and mineral salts from the soil.
- Some roots store food for the plant. Carrots, cassava and sweet potatoes are roots that store food, which is why we eat them.

### Stem
- Holds up the leaves so that they get sunlight, and holds up flowers and fruits.
- Carries water and mineral salts from the roots up to the leaves, and carries food made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.
- Some stems store food. Sugarcane stores sugar in its stem. An Irish potato is a swollen underground stem that stores food.

### Leaves
- Make food for the plant using sunlight, water and air. This is why most leaves are green, flat and wide: they catch plenty of sunlight.
- Allow air to move in and out of the plant through tiny openings.
- Give out extra water as water vapour.
- Some leaves are eaten as vegetables, such as sukuma wiki (kales), cabbage, spinach and cowpea leaves.

### Flowers
- Flowers are the parts used for reproduction. After a flower is pollinated, part of it grows into a fruit with seeds. Bright colours and sweet smells attract insects such as bees, which help in pollination.

### Fruits and seeds
- Fruits protect the seeds inside them.
- Seeds grow into new plants. Many fruits are eaten by animals and people, which helps to spread the seeds to new places.

All the parts work together. If the roots are cut, the leaves cannot get water and the plant wilts. If all the leaves are removed, the plant cannot make food.

## Key words
• function — the work that a part does
• absorb — to take in, as roots take in water from the soil
• mineral salts — substances in the soil that plants need to grow well
• wilt — to droop and go soft because of lack of water

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner puts a white flower with its stalk into a cup of water mixed with ink. After a day the petals have coloured lines. What does this show about the stem?

Working:
1. The coloured water moved up from the cup into the petals.
2. It travelled through the stem.

Answer: The stem carries water from the bottom of the plant to other parts.

### Example 2
Which part of each of these plants do we eat: cassava, sugarcane, sukuma wiki?

Working:
1. Cassava grows under the soil and stores food: root.
2. Sugarcane stores sugar in its tall stem: stem.
3. Sukuma wiki is eaten for its leaves: leaves.

Answer: Cassava – root, sugarcane – stem, sukuma wiki – leaves.

## Activity: Parts and their work
You will need: A whole weed or seedling with roots, A white flower or celery stalk, a cup of water and ink or food colour, Chart paper
1. In groups, observe the plant and point to each external part.
2. Put the flower or celery stalk in coloured water and leave it until the next lesson. Observe what happens.
3. Discuss the function of each part and write it on a chart: roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruits.
4. Present your chart to the class and listen to other groups' ideas.

## Practice
1. Give two functions of roots.
2. Which part of a plant makes food?
3. Why do many flowers have bright colours and sweet smells?
4. Name one stem that stores food.

## Summary
• Roots hold the plant and absorb water and mineral salts.
• The stem holds up the plant and carries water and food.
• Leaves make food; flowers help the plant reproduce; fruits protect seeds.

### Answers to practice
1. They hold the plant firmly in the soil and absorb water and mineral salts. Some also store food.
2. The leaves.
3. To attract insects such as bees that help in pollination.
4. Sugarcane (or Irish potato).

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Caring for plants
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: CARING FOR PLANTS
===========================

## What you will learn
• Explain why plants are important to people and animals.
• Describe ways of caring for plants at school and at home.

Curriculum outcomes: c) appreciate the need to care for plants

## Introduction
Think about your breakfast, your desk and the shade where you rest at break time. Plants gave you most of these things. If we want plants to keep helping us, we must take care of them.

## Notes
### Why we need plants
- **Food.** We eat roots (cassava, carrots), stems (sugarcane), leaves (sukuma wiki, spinach), fruits (mangoes, bananas) and seeds (maize, beans). Animals such as cows and goats feed on grass and leaves.
- **Air.** Green plants give out oxygen, which people and animals need to breathe.
- **Shade and shelter.** Trees give shade and act as windbreaks. Birds and many small animals live in trees.
- **Materials.** Timber for desks and houses, firewood, and fibres such as sisal and cotton come from plants.
- **Medicine.** Some medicines are made from plants.
- **Soil and water.** Roots hold soil together so that rain does not wash it away. Trees help protect the sources of rivers and streams.
- **Beauty.** Flowers and hedges make our compounds beautiful.

### How to care for plants
- Water young plants, especially in the dry season. Water in the morning or evening when it is cooler.
- Put mulch (dry grass or leaves) around plants to keep the soil moist.
- Add manure or compost so that plants get what they need to grow.
- Remove weeds that compete with plants for water and space.
- Put a fence or thorny branches around young trees to protect them from animals.
- Walk on paths and do not step on flower beds or seedlings.
- Do not pluck flowers, peel bark or break branches for fun.
- Plant new trees, especially to replace ones that have been cut down.

### Staying safe around plants
Some plants have thorns, sting (like the stinging nettle) or are poisonous. Do not touch or taste a plant you do not know, and wash your hands after working with plants.

## Key words
• mulch — dry grass or leaves spread on the soil around plants to keep it moist
• weed — a plant growing where it is not wanted
• windbreak — a line of trees or hedge that slows down strong wind

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The school has planted young trees near the playground, but goats keep eating them. Suggest a way to care for the trees.

Working:
1. The problem is animals eating the young trees.
2. The trees need protection until they are big.

Answer: Put a fence or thorny branches around each young tree.

## Activity: Adopt a plant
You will need: A young tree or potted plant in the school compound, Watering can or a used bottle, Dry grass for mulch
1. In your group, choose one young plant in the school compound to care for.
2. Remove the weeds around it, water it and spread mulch around it.
3. Make a simple chart to record each time you water it and how tall it grows.
4. Take turns so that every group member cares for the plant.
5. Tell the class how your plant changes over a few weeks.

## Practice
1. Give three reasons why plants are important.
2. Why should we put mulch around plants?
3. Name two things you should not do to plants in the school compound.

## Summary
• Plants give us food, oxygen, shade, materials and medicine.
• Care for plants by watering, mulching, weeding, adding manure and protecting them.
• Do not touch or taste plants you do not know.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: they give food, oxygen, shade, timber and firewood, medicine, they hold soil together, they make places beautiful.
2. Mulch keeps the soil moist so the plant does not dry up.
3. Any two: step on seedlings or flower beds, pluck flowers, peel bark, break branches.

questions.question: Which of these is a living thing?
questions.explanation: A bean plant grows, reproduces, removes waste, responds to changes and dies.

questions.question: A plant near a window bends towards the light. This shows that plants:
questions.explanation: Bending towards light is a response to a change in the environment.

questions.question: Name the characteristic of living things shown when a maize plant dries up after harvest.
questions.explanation: All living things die at the end of their lives.

questions.question: Which part of a plant holds it firmly in the soil?
questions.explanation: Roots grow into the soil and anchor the plant.

questions.question: Which part of a plant makes food?
questions.explanation: Green leaves make food using sunlight, water and air.

questions.question: Water moves from the roots to the leaves through the:
questions.explanation: The stem carries water and mineral salts up from the roots.

questions.question: Cassava and carrots are examples of plant parts that store food. Which part are they?
questions.explanation: Cassava and carrots are roots that store food.

questions.question: What is the main function of a flower?
questions.answer: Reproduction – it develops into a fruit with seeds.
questions.explanation: After pollination, part of the flower grows into a fruit that carries seeds.

questions.question: Which of these is a good way of caring for plants?
questions.explanation: Mulching keeps soil moist and watering gives the plant the water it needs.

questions.question: Give two reasons why we should care for plants.
questions.answer: Any two: plants give us food, oxygen, shade, timber, firewood, medicine, and they hold soil together.
questions.explanation: People and animals depend on plants in many ways.
